summary: A 1949 CIA intelligence memorandum assessing how Tripolitanians would react to an Italian UN trusteeship over Tripolitania, covering Arab hostility to Italian rule, British withdrawal, UN guarantees, and force requirements. It is mostly about the period before Libyan independence and does not concern Gaddafi-era sites.
facts: Estimates of force needed to re-establish Italian authority ranged from 13,100 minimum to 20,000-30,000 maximum with air cover; the British higher figure was ten times the roughly 3,000-man UK force then maintaining order in Tripolitania.
Italy agreed, at British insistence, to commit two infantry divisions, one cavalry (armored car) regiment, one carabinieri group, and one mobile carabinieri battalion to the trusteeship.
UK Foreign Office officials announced that if Italy became trustee, the UK would withdraw from Tripolitania immediately rather than cooperate in a phased transfer.

Tripolitanian leaders feared Italy would use a trusteeship to perpetuate itself and that Italian colonization would expropriate native lands; proposed UN guarantees covered native participation in government, independence after a time limit, and protection against land expropriation.
Municipal elections in Tripolitania had recently produced a victory for moderates, which Italians cited as evidence of likely Arab cooperation.
quote: The lower figure is Italian and presupposes British cooperation in the transfer.

summary: A 1983 private analytical memo speculates on the motives of North Korea, China, the Soviet Union and Libya behind a 1982 North Korean-Libyan friendship treaty, including possible arms transfers (MIG-23s) and nuclear aspirations. Libya encouraged Tuareg rebellion in Niger and offered haven and support to a leading oppositionist in Senegal.
Libya bribed Nigerian officials and supported political and religious groups there.
Libya encouraged rebellion by ethnic minorities in Mali.

facts: Eighteen US warplanes left Lakenheath Air Base in England on 14 April 1986; nine F-111s had the special mission targeting Qaddafi and his family, according to the article.
Each of the nine special-mission F-111s carried four 2,000-pound bombs; four of them had laser guidance malfunctions and aborted before reaching the target.
The article says more than 70 officials were interviewed and that the raid's targets listed officially were the command-and-control center and administrative buildings of El-Azziziya Barracks.
Qaddafi's last known location was at 11:15 P.M. Libyan time, about two hours and 45 minutes before the first bombs fell, while he was in his tent.
All eight of Qaddafi's children and his wife Safiya were hospitalized after the raid.

links.why: El-Azziziya Barracks in the article is the Bab al-Aziziya compound struck in the 1986 raid.

facts: Wilson said his import-export company, OSI-SA, was based in Tripoli and was one of the few foreign firms still doing business in Libya after nationalization.
